title: Shortcut Conflict shown when there's no documented conflict.
summary: PowerToys reports a system shortcut conflict for Color Picker Win+Shift+C even though the shortcut still works; the runner is conflating RegisterHotKey conflicts with low-level-hook hotkeys.
next_action: This issue was selected as the single full implementation-grade design for the batch; the artifact contains a converged hook-aware conflict-detection design.

confidence.rationale: The current code paths directly explain how a low-level-hook module can work while the RegisterHotKey-based detector still labels it as a system conflict.

linked_work.title: A conflict shortcut key of unknown origin in PowerToys shortcut conflict window

judgment.rationale: The issue has a current, repo-local design path: make system-conflict detection aware of whether a module uses the low-level keyboard hook or RegisterHotKey.
evidence: The reporter sees a system shortcut conflict for Win+Shift+C, yet Color Picker still opens and works.

Color Picker exposes its activation shortcut through get_hotkeys() in src/modules/colorPicker/ColorPicker/dllmain.cpp, which PowertoyModule wires to CentralizedKeyboardHook::SetHotkeyAction in src/runner/powertoy_module.cpp.
HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey() in src/runner/hotkey_conflict_detector.cpp uses RegisterHotKey(nullptr, ...) as its system-conflict probe.
Issue 50402 reports another unexplained shortcut-conflict entry in the same PowerToys surface, suggesting the problem is broader than a single key.
judgment.recommended_action: Approve the hook-aware conflict-detection design below and implement it in the runner so low-level-hook modules stop surfacing false system conflicts.

fix_assessment.rationale: No current fix attempt or merged PR addresses the mismatch between low-level-hook hotkeys and RegisterHotKey-based system-conflict detection.

issue_context.summary: The report is a false-positive shortcut-conflict bug: Color Picker Win+Shift+C still works, but PowerToys labels it as a system conflict and links to Windows shortcut documentation that does not list that chord.
known_information: The issue was filed against PowerToys 0.101.2362 stable on Windows 11 build 26200.
The configured shortcut is Win+Shift+C for Color Picker.
The shortcut still functions to open Color Picker; the bug is the conflict warning itself.
A second thread, Issue 50402, describes another unexplained shortcut-conflict entry in the same UI.
inferences: The warning is likely generated from a generic conflict heuristic rather than from the actual activation path used by Color Picker.
Because the shortcut still works, the current system-conflict classification is more likely overstating a RegisterHotKey-only reservation than identifying a real activation blocker for this module.
issue_context.analysis: The critical clue is that Color Picker is not activated through RegisterHotKey. It uses the centralized low-level keyboard hook, so the hotkey detector’s RegisterHotKey probe can report a conflict that does not actually block the feature. That is exactly the symptom the reporter sees.
initial_investigation: PowertoyModule::update_hotkeys() routes get_hotkeys() modules into CentralizedKeyboardHook::SetHotkeyAction in src/runner/powertoy_module.cpp.
Color Picker defines its activation shortcut through get_hotkeys() in src/modules/colorPicker/ColorPicker/dllmain.cpp.
HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey() in src/runner/hotkey_conflict_detector.cpp decides system conflicts by probing RegisterHotKey(nullptr, ...).
The dashboard consumes sysConflictHotkeyMap as real system conflicts, so a probe mismatch becomes a visible false-positive card.

actions.label: Approve hook-aware shortcut conflict fix
actions.note: This issue was selected as the batch’s single full implementation-grade design and is ready for implementation if approved.

proposed_fixes.title: Make system hotkey conflict detection registration-aware
proposed_fixes.root_cause: The runner currently treats RegisterHotKey failure as a definitive system conflict for every PowerToys hotkey, even when that module actually activates through the centralized low-level keyboard hook rather than RegisterHotKey. That makes hook-driven shortcuts like Color Picker show a false system conflict while they continue to work.
plan: Track whether each module hotkey came from get_hotkeys() (low-level hook path) or GetHotkeyEx() (RegisterHotKey path).
Use documented reserved-shortcut checks for both paths, but only use the RegisterHotKey probe for modules whose real activation path depends on RegisterHotKey.
Keep active dashboard/system-conflict output tied to true blocking conflicts, and add regression tests for low-level-hook hotkeys like Color Picker.
verification: Set Color Picker to Win+Shift+C on Windows 11 and verify the shortcut still works without an active system conflict card.
Verify a RegisterHotKey-based module still reports a system conflict when the OS truly blocks registration.
Verify in-app conflict detection between two PowerToys modules still works unchanged.

confidence.rationale: The mismatch is directly visible in current code: active module hotkeys can be low-level-hook based while the detector still relies on RegisterHotKey semantics.

design.root_cause: System-conflict detection is not aware of the module hotkey transport. For get_hotkeys()-based modules, PowerToys uses the centralized low-level keyboard hook, but HotkeyConflictManager still calls RegisterHotKey to decide whether the shortcut is a system conflict. A RegisterHotKey failure therefore becomes a visible conflict even when the real module path still works.
evidence: Observed: Color Picker registers its shortcut through get_hotkeys() in src/modules/colorPicker/ColorPicker/dllmain.cpp and does not use GetHotkeyEx().
Observed: PowertoyModule::update_hotkeys() wires get_hotkeys() entries to CentralizedKeyboardHook::SetHotkeyAction in src/runner/powertoy_module.cpp.

Observed: HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey() in src/runner/hotkey_conflict_detector.cpp calls RegisterHotKey(nullptr, hotkeyId, modifiers, hotkey.key) and treats ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED as a system conflict.
Observed: DashboardViewModel renders runner-provided sysConflictHotkeyMap entries as active shortcut conflicts.
Inferred: Win+Shift+C is reaching a RegisterHotKey-only reservation/legacy overlap on Windows 11, but that reservation does not block Color Picker’s hook-driven activation path.

affected_files.purpose: Add hotkey-registration metadata so conflict evaluation can distinguish low-level-hook hotkeys from RegisterHotKey-based hotkeys.
Implement registration-aware system-conflict checks and keep active conflict maps limited to true blocking conflicts.
Pass the correct hotkey-registration kind from get_hotkeys() versus GetHotkeyEx() call sites.
Add regression coverage for low-level-hook false positives and preserve RegisterHotKey-based conflict behavior.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: Conflict records only track the hotkey, module name, and hotkey ID; the detector has no way to tell whether the module uses the centralized low-level hook or RegisterHotKey.
implementation_steps.change: Add an explicit registration-kind enum (for example LowLevelHook vs RegisterHotKey) to the hotkey conflict model and thread it through the AddHotkey / HasConflict pipeline.
edge_cases: Disabled-module hotkeys kept in disabledHotkeys must preserve the registration kind so re-enable does not change behavior.
Hash/equality helpers must include registrationKind only if conflict records from different transports should remain distinct in sets.
tests: Unit-test that AddHotkey stores and rehydrates registrationKind through disable/enable transitions.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: Both low-level-hook get_hotkeys() entries and GetHotkeyEx() entries call HotkeyConflictManager::AddHotkey without telling the manager which transport they actually use.
implementation_steps.change: Pass LowLevelHook from update_hotkeys() and RegisterHotKey from UpdateHotkeyEx() so the detector can evaluate system conflicts against the same activation model the module really uses.
edge_cases: Modules that expose both styles over time during settings changes must clear and rebuild the old records to avoid stale conflict state.
No behavior change should occur for in-app conflict detection across modules sharing the same shortcut.
tests: Add a runner unit or fake integration test that exercises both call paths and confirms they produce different registration kinds.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: Every hotkey uses the same RegisterHotKey-based system-conflict probe, so low-level-hook modules inherit false-positive system conflicts from a different transport model.
implementation_steps.change: Split system-conflict evaluation into (a) a small explicit reserved-shortcut check that applies to all modules, and (b) the existing RegisterHotKey probe that only applies to RegisterHotKey-based modules. Do not populate sysConflictHotkeyMap for low-level-hook modules solely because the RegisterHotKey probe failed.
edge_cases: Keep the existing in-app conflict ordering so two PowerToys modules sharing a hotkey still surface as in-app conflicts first.
Seed MatchesKnownWindowsReservedHotkey with only clearly reserved/sensitive chords to avoid introducing a different false-positive class.
If the dashboard later needs a softer “possible overlap” concept for low-level-hook shortcuts, add it as a new non-actionable metadata field rather than reusing SystemConflict.
tests: Regression: a low-level-hook hotkey with a mocked RegisterHotKey failure does not land in sysConflictHotkeyMap.
Regression: a RegisterHotKey-based hotkey with the same mocked failure still lands in sysConflictHotkeyMap.
Regression: explicit reserved shortcuts remain blocked for both transports.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: The unit tests only cover a basic in-app conflict case and do not pin the low-level-hook versus RegisterHotKey distinction.
implementation_steps.change: Add deterministic tests around the new registration-kind split, plus a dashboard-facing regression that models Color Picker-like low-level-hook behavior.
edge_cases: Tests should not depend on real OS hotkey availability; inject or abstract the RegisterHotKey probe so unit results stay stable on CI.
Cover module disable/re-enable so stored registration kinds do not regress after state changes.
tests: Runner unit tests for low-level-hook false positives, RegisterHotKey true conflicts, and preserved in-app conflicts.

verify: Open PowerToys Settings, assign Color Picker to Win+Shift+C on Windows 11, and verify Color Picker still opens while the dashboard shows no active system conflict.
Assign two PowerToys modules the same shortcut and verify the dashboard still shows an in-app conflict.
Use or simulate a RegisterHotKey-based module with a truly blocked shortcut and verify the system-conflict card still appears.
Run the runner hotkey conflict unit tests covering the new registration-kind logic.
risks: A too-small reserved-shortcut list could hide warnings for genuinely sensitive OS shortcuts on low-level-hook modules.
A too-large reserved-shortcut list would recreate false positives under a different name; the list must stay intentionally conservative and documented.
Disabled/re-enabled modules must preserve registration-kind metadata or conflicts may appear to flicker after settings changes.
alternatives: Keep the current RegisterHotKey probe but rename the UI copy. Rejected because the issue is not only wording; the dashboard is surfacing a false active conflict for a working shortcut.
Drop all system-conflict detection for low-level-hook modules. Rejected because PowerToys still needs a place to block clearly reserved/sensitive Windows chords.
Move all modules to RegisterHotKey. Rejected because many existing modules intentionally rely on the centralized low-level hook and would lose current behavior.

design_review.signoff: No blocking objections after separating low-level-hook activation from RegisterHotKey-only conflict probing.
non_blocking_notes: If the product wants to keep softer overlap hints for low-level-hook shortcuts, add a new non-actionable metadata concept later instead of overloading SystemConflict.
Any reserved-shortcut list should be documented beside the runner logic to avoid drift with the Settings UI tooltip text.
